SUBJECT: Conditional Use Permit (CUP 25-06)

PROJECT PROPOSAL/REQUEST: A request for approval of a Conditional Use Permit (CUP) to allow
the sale of alcohol (ABC License Type 41 - beer and wine) for on-site consumption in conjunction with an
existing restaurant (Kazan BBQ) located at 8730 Garfield Avenue.

Project Overview

  General Plan Designation: Mixed Use-Commercial/Industrial
   District: El Paseo / South Gate Towne Center (Sub-area 1)

  Zoning: Regional Commercial (RC)

  Project Location: 8730 Garfield Avenue

  Assessor’s Parcel Number: 6232-003-015

  Applicant: Valley Lin

BACKGROUND:

  Site Characteristics: The subject site is an existing dine-in Korean BBQ restaurant (Kazan BBQ) located
  at the southwest corner of the El Paseo shopping center (midblock from Firestone Boulevard). The
  commercial building is located on an approximately 7.89-acre parcel, one of several comprising the El
  Paseo shopping center. The subject site is bounded by Garfield Avenue to the west, and commercial
  buildings to the north, east, and south.
  The site will utilize parking shared with other properties within the shopping center.
  The existing building measures 5,759 square feet (SF); the restaurant will feature approximately 3,064
  square feet of indoor dining and 1,178 SF of outdoor dining. The remainder of the building is used for
  kitchen and storage.

  Surroundings: To the north of the property is the South Pacific Railroad and the jurisdictional boundary
  between the cities of South Gate and Bell Gardens; to the east of the shopping center is the Rio Hondo
  River; to the south is the Crossroads commercial center; and to the west is a manufacturing use, Tesoro
  Logistic Operations.

ANALYSIS:

  Municipal Code Requirements for a CUP: Pursuant to South Gate Municipal Code (SGMC) Section
  11.21.030, Table 11.21-4 (Commercial Industrial Zones Allowed Land Uses), the sales of alcoholic

April 7, 2026

  beverages for on-site consumption in conjunction with a restaurant may be permitted provided a
  Conditional Use Permit (CUP) is granted by the Planning Commission.

  Required findings for a CUP: Pursuant to SGMC Section 11.52.030, before a CUP may be granted, the
  Planning Commission (or the City Council on appeal) shall make all the following findings, as
  applicable to the property:

    Approval of the CUP is consistent with and will not adversely affect the intent and purpose of
  this title or the city’s General Plan.

    The design and development of the land use and conditions of the CUP are compatible with the
  existing and future land uses of the applicable zone.

    Approval of the CUP would not result in detrimental impacts to adjacent properties or to the
  character or function of the neighborhood.

  Municipal Code Conditions of Approval for Alcoholic Beverage Sales: Pursuant to SGMC Section
  11.42.070, any CUP for alcoholic beverage sales shall include minimum mandatory conditions which
  are included in the proposed Resolution.

Business Operations

The business is currently operating seven days a week: Monday through Friday from 4 PM to 10 PM and
weekends from 12 PM to 11 PM. The applicant is applying for a new Type 41 license from the Department
of Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) to serve beer and wine to patrons as part of the dining service.
Offering alcoholic beverages is intended to enhance the dining atmosphere and improve the overall guest
experience. By providing this option, the restaurant hopes to attract customers who enjoy having a drink
with their meals and appeal to a wider audience. In addition, the ability to serve alcohol could contribute to
increased revenue for the establishment.

Alcohol will be offered Monday – Friday from 4 PM to 9 PM and weekends from 12 PM to 10 PM; the
sale of alcohol will cease one hour before closing. The applicant proposes to offer bottled alcohol as well
as beer on tap. Bottled alcohol is proposed to be stored within a walk-in cooler located at the rear of the
restaurant while beer on tap will be located next to the walk-in cooler, also at the rear of the restaurant. A
standard condition is included that alcohol may only be consumed within the enclosed building on premises
and in permitted outdoor seating areas for on-sale uses.

Security measures are not currently proposed; however, a condition of approval will require the applicant
to install a video surveillance system to monitor the premises on a 24-hour basis and provide recordings to
the Police Department upon request. With the condition, including other standard conditions of approval,
it is anticipated that the proposed sale of beer and wine will not cause nuisances or compromise the public
health, safety, and welfare.

Additionally, staff recommends a condition requiring that all alcohol-related signage and advertisements
be displayed only within the interior of the business, away from storefront windows, and placed above
child-height eye level. This measure is intended to reduce visibility of alcohol promotions to minors and to
support a family-oriented environment consistent with the character of the restaurant. Alcohol sales signage
will not be visible from the public street or parking lot.

Off-Street Parking

Pursuant to SGMC Section 11.33.030, the minimum requirement for a dine-in restaurant measuring more
than 4,000 SF in floor area is 40 spaces plus 1 per 50 SF over the 4,000 SF. That means a total of 75 parking
spaces would normally be required for the subject restaurant.

The restaurant use and its parking area were originally established prior to the City’s 2015 adoption of the
current zoning code and as part of the Towne Center Phase I and Phase II project. The shopping center has
since been renamed to El Paseo. Since the current number of parking spaces complied with former zoning
requirements, the current parking area and spaces for this use are considered legal nonconforming.
Additionally, during the Towne Center Phase I and II project, a parking study was conducted to establish
that the parking space provided would suffice for the intended restaurant land use along with all other
commercial uses of the center.

The proposed project includes no physical development and only includes an added use of alcohol sales for
on-site consumption in conjunction with an existing dine-in restaurant. As such, no additional off-street
parking is required.

CUP Analysis

A CUP for the sale of alcohol at a restaurant requires approval by the Planning Commission. In granting
approval of a CUP, the Planning Commission shall make all the following findings, as applicable to the
property, as found in SGMC Section 11.52.030. Justification for each finding is included in the proposed
Resolution.

A. Approval of the CUP is consistent with and will not adversely affect the intent and purpose of this title
  or the City’s General Plan.

B. The design and development of the land use and conditions of the CUP are compatible with the existing
  and future land uses of the applicable zone.

C. Approval of the CUP would not result in detrimental impacts to adjacent properties or to the character
  or function of the neighborhood.

ENVIRONMENTAL ANALYSIS:

In accordance with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), this project qualifies for a
categorical exemption under CEQA Guidelines Section 15301, (Class 1) “Existing Facilities”, in that the
project will not result in any alterations or expansion to the existing buildings within the project site.
Further, no exceptions to the exemption apply; there is no reasonable possibility that the activity will have
a significant effect on the environment due to unusual circumstances. The property is already developed,
and the proposed use is only for the sale of alcohol (beer and wine) for on-site consumption in conjunction
with an existing dine-in restaurant.

DEPARTMENT COMMENTS:

Staff routed the project for comments to several City Departments including the Police Department, Public
Works Department, and the Building & Safety Division. The conditions of approval contained in the
attached Resolution include conditions based on comments received from other City Departments.

The California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control confirmed that although the census tract is over-
concentrated, an additional license may be granted. The census tract recommends a total of 3 on-sale
licenses be allowed; currently there are 7 active licenses.

CONCLUSION:

Based on the above analysis, staff has determined that with the recommended conditions of approval, the
proposed project will comply with the SGMC, and all the required findings in support of a CUP will be
made.

RECOMMENDATION:

Based on the evidence presented, Staff recommends that the Planning Commission find that the project is
Categorically Exempt from the CEQA under Section 15301, (Class 1) “Existing Facilities”, make the
required findings and requirements set forth in the South Gate Municipal Code, and approve the
application for a Conditional Use Permit (CUP 25-06) subject to the conditions of approval contained
in the attached Resolution No. 2026-04 and/or other conditions that the Planning Commission may wish to
impose.

A RESOLUTION OF THE PLANNING COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF SOUTH GATE,
APPROVING A CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT (CUP NO. 25-06), TO ALLOW THE SALE OF
ALCOHOL (ABC LICENSE TYPE 41 - BEER AND WINE) FOR ON-SITE CONSUMPTION IN
CONJUNCTION WITH AN EXISTING RESTAURANT (“KAZAN BBQ”) LOCATED AT 8730
GARFIELD AVENUE, IN THE URBAN NEIGHBORHOOD (UN) ZONE, AND FINDING THE
PROJECT CATEGORICALLY EXEMPT FROM THE CALIFORNIA ENVIRONMENTAL
QUALITY ACT.

  WHEREAS, Valley Lin (“the Applicant”), on behalf of Kazan BBQ, filed a complete application
requesting the approval of a Conditional Use Permit (CUP No. 25-06) described herein (“Application”);
and

  WHEREAS, the Application pertains to an approximately 7.89-acre property with Los Angeles
County Assessor’s Parcel Number 6232-003-015, more commonly known as 8730 Garfield Avenue, South
Gate, California (“Property”); and

  WHEREAS, the Applicant requests approval of CUP No. 25-06 to allow the sale of alcohol (ABC
License Type 41 - beer and wine) for on-site consumption in conjunction with an existing restaurant
(“Kazan BBQ”). Pursuant to South Gate Municipal Code (SGMC) Section 11.21.030, Table 11.21-3
(Allowed Land Uses, Urban Mixed Use Zones), the sale of alcoholic beverages for on-site consumption in
conjunction with a restaurant may be permitted provided a CUP is granted by the Planning Commission;
and

  WHEREAS, Pursuant to South Gate Municipal Code Section 11.52.030, before a CUP may be
granted, the Planning Commission shall make all of the following findings, as applicable to the property:

  (a) Approval of the CUP is consistent with and will not adversely affect the intent and purpose of
  this title or the city’s General Plan.

  (b) The design and development of the land use and conditions of the CUP are compatible with the
  existing and future land uses of the applicable zone.

  (c) Approval of the CUP would not result in detrimental impacts to adjacent properties or to the
  character or function of the neighborhood.

  WHEREAS, notice of the Planning Commission regular public hearing of April 7, 2026, was
published in compliance with State law in a local newspaper of general circulation. In addition, a public
notice was mailed 10 days in advance of the hearing to each property owner, occupants and resident within
a 1,000-foot radius of the project site, indicating the date and time of the public hearing in accordance with
California Government Code 65091; and

  WHEREAS, on April 7, 2026, the Planning Commission held a regular public hearing to receive
public testimony and other evidence regarding the Application, including without limitation, information
provided to the Planning Commission by City staff and public testimony; and

  WHEREAS, this Resolution and its findings are made based upon evidence presented to the
Commission at its public hearing including, without limitation, the staff report submitted by the Community
Development Department; and

NOW, THEREFORE, THE PLANNING COMMISSION DOES HEREBY FIND, DETERMINE
AND DECLARE AS FOLLOWS:

SECTION 1.  All of the facts set forth in the recitals are true and correct and are incorporated herein by
reference.

SECTION 2. Based upon substantial evidence presented to this Planning Commission during the public
hearing conducted with regard to the Application, including written staff reports, verbal testimony, site
plans, and Conditions of Approval (“Conditions”) attached hereto as Exhibit “A,” the Planning Commission
hereby specifically finds as follows:

  A. Approval of the CUP is consistent with and will not adversely affect the intent and purpose
  of this title or the city’s General Plan in that the Community Design Element encourages
  the development of diverse and vibrant dining and entertainment options within
  designated commercial areas, which enhance the local economy and provide a range of
  services for residents and visitors.

  Specifically, Objective CD 2.3, Policy P.4 specifies that “the City should encourage and
  promote retail and service-oriented uses that provide opportunities to bring community
  members together. Such uses include cafés, restaurants, farmers markets, and theaters.”
  The addition of alcohol sales will enhance customer experience and is expected to
  increase sales. Thus, the approval of this CUP is consistent with the goals of the City’s
  General Plan.

  B. The design and development of the land use and conditions of the CUP are compatible with
  the existing and future land uses of the applicable zone in that the restaurant is already
  an established business within a fully developed site, and the requested ABC license
  (Type 41) will not alter the existing physical structure or operations of the restaurant.
  The proposed use is consistent with the current zoning regulations and compatible with
  the surrounding land uses, which include commercial and retail establishments within
  the designated zone.

  The addition of the requested license will not introduce new incompatible land uses or
  development impacts, as the site is already operating as a shopping center with adequate
  infrastructure to support its current and proposed activities. The conditions of the CUP
  will ensure that the proposed alcohol-related uses are appropriately managed, preserving
  the compatibility with existing uses and allowing for future development consistent with
  the zoning district's objectives. Therefore, the project complies with the intent of the
  zoning regulations and the future land use goals of the area.

  C. Approval of the CUP would not result in detrimental impacts to adjacent properties or to
  the character or function of the neighborhood in that the restaurant is an established
  business within an existing commercial property located in an area designated for retail
  and mixed-use development. The proposed ABC license (Type 41) will not introduce
  incompatible activities that would negatively affect adjacent properties or the overall
  character of the neighborhood. The restaurant’s existing operations are compatible with
  surrounding land uses, and the requested license is consistent with the site's long-
  standing commercial function.

   With recommended conditions of approval, including the requirement for a 24-hour
  video surveillance system available to the Police Department upon request, the proposed
  alcohol-related use will be controlled to minimize any adverse impacts, and the overall
  function of the neighborhood—characterized by retail, commercial, and community-
  serving businesses—will remain intact. Therefore, the approval of this CUP will not
  disrupt the established character of the area or adversely affect neighboring properties.

SECTION 3. The Planning Commission reviewed the project’s environmental impacts under the
California Environmental Quality Act (California Public Resources Code Section 21000, et seq., “CEQA”)
and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 California Code of Regulations Section 15000, et seq., the
“CEQA Guidelines”) and finds the project to be exempt under a Class 1 Categorical Exemption pursuant
to section 15301 (Existing Facilities) of the CEQA Guidelines (Title 14, Chapter 3 of the California Code
of Regulations). Further, no exceptions to the exemption apply; there is no reasonable possibility that the
activity will have a significant effect on the environment due to unusual circumstances. The property is
already developed and the proposed use is an ABC license for ancillary alcohol sales in conjunction with
an existing dine-in restaurant.

SECTION 4. The Planning Commission hereby approves CUP No. 25-06 subject to the execution and
fulfillment of Conditions of Approval set forth in Exhibit “A” attached to this Resolution.

  PLANNING COMMISSION

  For the Regular Meeting of: April 7, 2026
Community Development Director:

SUBJECT: APPEAL OF DIRECTOR DETERMINATION — LAND USE CLASSIFICATION FOR
A PROPOSED SELF-SERVICE LAUNDROMAT AT 4382–4390 TWEEDY BOULEVARD;
APPELANT: EMILIA KERIAN - (PL NO. 26-0107)

RECOMMENDATION:

Staff recommends that the Planning Commission:

  1. Consider the applicant's appeal and determine if the proposed self-service laundromat at 4382–4390
  Tweedy Boulevard is most appropriately classified as "Personal Services, General" under South Gate
  Municipal Code Section 11.60, and that such use is a permitted use within the TMU-2 (Tweedy
  Mixed-Use 2) zone pursuant to the Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan land use table. Resolution No.
  2026-05, Appeal denial, was prepared based on the original Director’s land use determination.

BACKGROUND:

Project Description
Daniel Leal (Applicant), proposes to operate a fully self-service coin-operated laundromat at 4382, 4386,
and 4390 Tweedy Boulevard (collectively, the Project Site), encompassing approximately 7,000 square feet
of ground-floor commercial space in the TMU-2 zone of the Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan. The proposed
facility would consist of commercial-grade washers and dryers operated directly by customers, staffed
attendants for customer service and facility maintenance, accessory retail sales of laundry products
(detergent, fabric softener, dryer sheets), and no drop-off or pick-up laundry service — customers bring
their own items, operate machines themselves, and take finished laundry at the time of service. The facility
is proposed to serve an estimated 700 to 1,000 customer visits per week, with typical customer dwell times
of 60 to 90 minutes.

Site and Zoning Context
The project site consists of three contiguous storefronts on the south side of Tweedy Boulevard that are
currently vacant. The tenant spaces were previously occupied by the Children’s Counseling Center, Casa
de Vape, Sixthstar Computers, Cyber Café, and Peter Pan Hair Salon. The property is located within the
TMU-2 zone of the Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan (South Gate Municipal Code Chapter 11.28). The site
has been substantially vacant for approximately five years. Tweedy Boulevard is the City's primary
commercial corridor and the Specific Plan was adopted to guide mixed-use revitalization of the corridor
with active ground-floor uses, extended customer dwell times, and pedestrian-oriented design. Fiesta Coin
Laundry is an existing laundromat at 4409 Tweedy Blvd about 250 feet from the proposed laundromat.

  22
   Figure 1: Proposed Laundromat 4382-4390 Tweedy Boulevard

History of the Use Classification Issue
The term "laundromat" does not appear in the current South Gate Zoning Code (Title 11). Prior to a
comprehensive zoning update in 2015, laundromats were explicitly listed as a conditionally permitted use
(CUP) in applicable commercial zones regardless of size (Ordinance 1192 adopted in 1972). Laundry
agencies were listed as permitted by right in the previous Zoning Code, but without a definition or a size
restriction. The 2015 zoning update removed the “laundromat” term from Title 11, and the Code now
identifies two related but distinct uses: 1) "Dry Cleaning/Laundry, Agency" and 2) "Dry Cleaning/Laundry,
Plant” without specifically addressing self-service coin-operated laundry facilities.

Following pre-application meetings in April and May 2025, the applicant contends that the City Planning
staff confirmed to the applicant that a laundromat would be permitted at the project site with no stated size
restriction, the applicant executed a 10-year lease (with two 5-year renewal options) for the project site on
May 2, 2025. The applicant subsequently invested substantial financial resources in pre-development
activities, architectural design, and lease obligations (base rent of $12,725.50 per month) in reliance on those
representations.

In July 2025, the City's Public Works Department placed a hold on plan check review pending resolution of
a Planning land use issue. The Community Development Director determined that the most applicable land
use classification for a laundromat under the current Code is "Dry Cleaning/Laundry, Agency or Plant,"
with the operative distinction being the 2,500-square-foot threshold separating an Agency from a Plant.
Because the proposed laundromat is approximately 7,000 square feet, the Director classified the proposed
use as a Laundry Plant.

The Director further determined that "Dry Cleaning/Laundry, Plant" is not a listed permitted use in the
Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan land use table, and therefore, the 7,000-square-foot laundromat could not
be approved in the TMU-2 zone. The Director offered the Applicant the opportunity to appeal this
determination to the Planning Commission.

  23
 DISCUSSION/ANALYSIS:

Director's Determination and Basis for Appeal
The Director determined that the proposed self-service laundromat is most similar to a "Dry
Cleaning/Laundry" use, as defined in South Gate Municipal Code Section 11.60.070, which distinguishes
between two subcategories:

    Agency: A facility where materials are dropped off and picked up for cleaning service, or cleaned
  on site through either conventional laundry or chemical processes, where the facility is less than
  2,500 square feet and no material collected at other dry cleaning or laundry agencies are brought for
  cleaning.
    Plant: A facility greater than 2,500 square feet, or that processes items collected from other retail
  locations, where clothing and similar items are cleaned through either conventional laundry or
  chemical processes.

The Director determined that the “agency” and “plant” definition indicates “that materials are dropped off
and picked up for cleaning service, or cleaned on site through either conventional laundry,” which are similar
laundromat activities operating as a self-service facility where customers utilize laundry appliances as a
conventional cleaning service occurring on-site. Because the proposed laundromat is approximately 7,000
square feet, the Director classified it as a Laundry Plant. The Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan land use table
identifies "Dry Cleaning/Laundry, Agency" as a permitted use in the TMU-2 zone but does not list "Dry
Cleaning/Laundry, Plant." The Director therefore concluded that the proposed use is not permitted in the
TMU-2 zone at the proposed size. Staff suspects that the omission of "Dry Cleaning/Laundry, Plant” from
the Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan land use table was intentional to limit the size of laundry facilities that
could preclude retail and dining establishments along Tweedy Boulevard, although this cannot be verified
from existing specific plan documentation.

The Director acknowledges that there is genuine ambiguity in applying the Laundry Agency/Plant
framework to a self-service coin-operated laundromat. The Director has separately briefed the Planning
Commission on a pending code amendment that would add "laundromat" as an explicitly listed conditionally
permitted use in the Urban Mixed-Use zones with a 2,500-foot distance separation; however, that
amendment is months away from adoption. Under the proposed draft code amendment, the proposed
laundromat would not be permitted due to the distance of approximately 250 feet from the existing
laundromat. The Director had outlined the appeal process as the mechanism by which the Applicant could
consider.

The Applicant, AquaLoop Laundromat LLC, has appealed the Director's determination on the grounds that
a self-service laundromat is not properly classified as a Dry Cleaning/Laundry use under any definition and
is more correctly classified as "Personal Services, General," a permitted use by right in the TMU-2 zone.

Applicant's Appeal Justification
The Applicant's appeal justification (Attachment 2) advances two primary arguments: (A) the Dry
Cleaning/Laundry definitions do not describe a self-service laundromat, and (B) a self-service laundromat
satisfies the definition of Personal Services, General and is consistent with the listed examples and analogous
uses under that definition.

  24
 A. Misclassification as Dry Cleaning/Laundry — Agency or Plant
The Applicant argues that both the Agency and Plant definitions describe a business that performs cleaning
services on behalf of customers. In both definitions, materials are “dropped off and picked up,” and the
business cleans items through “conventional laundry or chemical processes.” The 2,500-square-foot
threshold was designed to distinguish a small drop-off retail location (Agency) from a large service-
processing facility (Plant), both of which involve the business performing the cleaning.

A self-service laundromat fits neither description. No items are dropped off. No items are picked up by staff.
The business does not perform any cleaning. Customers bring their own laundry, operate commercial
washing and drying machines themselves, and take their items when the cycle is complete. The 2,500-
square-foot threshold has no logical application to a self-service model, because that threshold was designed
to regulate the scale of a laundry service processing operation, not the customer capacity of a self-service
facility.

B. Correct Classification as Personal Services, General
The Applicant argues that the proposed laundromat satisfies each element of the Personal Services, General
definition in South Gate Municipal Code Section 11.60:
   "Personal Services" (land use) means any place of business providing services and accessory retail
  sales of products related to the services provided.
   "General" means establishments providing nonmedical services to individuals as a primary use.

The Applicant's analysis is as follows:

  1. Nonmedical service to individuals as primary use. Customers visit the facility to perform a personal
  task of washing and drying their clothing and household textiles. The business provides the service
  of making commercial-grade equipment available in a clean, professionally maintained, and staffed
  environment. This is a nonmedical service to individuals as a primary use.
  2. Accessory retail sales of products related to the services provided. Laundromats customarily sell
  detergent, fabric softener, dryer sheets, stain removers, and related products, mirroring how a barber
  shop sells hair care products, a tailor sells thread and notions, or a fitness center sells supplements.
  3. The listed examples are non-exhaustive. The Code states that general personal service uses "may
  also include" the listed examples (barber/beauty shop, clothing rental, home electronics and small
  appliance repair, locksmith, pet grooming, shoe repair, tailor, waxing shop) and uses the term
  "include", not "limited to." A self-service laundromat is an unlisted but qualifying example under
  this non-exhaustive framework.
  4. The fitness center analogy. The Personal Services definition already encompasses fitness and health
  facilities, defined as any place of business providing facilities devoted to health, beauty, and
  relaxation, including health or physical fitness centers. A fitness center provides commercial
  equipment in a maintained facility; customers arrive, operate the equipment themselves, remain on-
  site for an extended period, and depart. A self-service laundromat operates on an identical model
  characterized by commercial equipment, self-operation by the customer, extended dwell time, and
  no service performed by the operator on the customer's behalf. If a facility where customers use
  equipment and leave is a personal service when that equipment is a treadmill, it is equally a personal
  service when that equipment is a washing machine.

  25
 Zoning Code Text Ambiguity
The Director has acknowledged that there is genuine ambiguity in classifying a self-service laundromat
under the current Code. The Dry Cleaning/Laundry Agency and Plant definitions were drafted for businesses
that perform cleaning services for customers, such as dry cleaners, linen service providers, and commercial
laundry operators. The definition does not capture the self-service model. The applicability of the 2,500-
square-foot threshold to a coin-operated laundromat is particularly unclear, as that threshold may have been
designed to regulate the scale of service processing operations, not the customer-facing floor area of a self-
service facility. The Director contacted a previous City planner present during the zoning code update in
2015 to understand the reason for the laundromat classification change. The planner was not completely
certain for the justification of the change, but believed the intent was to prohibit laundromats citywide by
omitting the land use classification entirely.

Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan Policy Consistency
The proposed laundromat is consistent with the goals and policies of the Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan.
The Specific Plan was adopted to encourage active, pedestrian-oriented ground-floor uses along the corridor,
reduce vacancy, attract businesses that generate sustained foot traffic, and serve the daily needs of a dense,
renter-majority neighborhood. The proposed project would:

    Activate three contiguous storefronts that have been substantially vacant for approximately five
  years, in a corridor with approximately 30 vacant storefronts along Tweedy Boulevard.
    Generate an estimated 700 to 1,000 customer visits per week, with 60 to 90 minute dwell times per
  visit, supporting sustained pedestrian activity and ancillary commercial vitality.
    Serve an essential daily need for residents in a high-density, renter-majority neighborhood where in-
  unit laundry is limited and access to commercial laundry facilities is a significant quality-of-life
  concern.
    Represent a 10-year lease commitment (with options to extend to 20 years), providing long-term
  corridor stability and anchoring contiguous storefronts under active use.
    Be designed as a modern, attended facility with transparent storefront design and high-quality
  finishes, consistent with the Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan's design standards for active ground-
  floor commercial uses.

CONCLUSION:

Based on the foregoing analysis, staff recommends that the Planning Commission consider the applicant’s
appeal justification that a self-service coin-operated laundromat, as proposed at 4382–4390 Tweedy
Boulevard, is most accurately classified as "Personal Services, General" under South Gate Municipal Code
Section 11.60, rather than "Dry Cleaning/Laundry, Agency or Plant." The Director has acknowledged that
there is genuine ambiguity in classifying a self-service laundromat under the current Code but has not
changed its perspective for the land use determination and is the reason that a code amendment to clarify
the laundromat use classification is under consideration. Under the current Director’s land use
determination, the applicant would still be able to operate a laundromat of 2,500 square feet or less in the
TMU-2 zone.

A Commission determination to grant the appeal would allow the Applicant to proceed with permitting and
buildout of the proposed facility in the TMU-2 zone as a permitted use by right under the Personal Services,

  26
 General classification, without further land use entitlement. A Planning Commission resolution has been
prepared to deny the appeal based on the Director’s determination of the laundromat use. If the Planning
Commission were to grant the appeal, staff would prepare the corresponding resolution for the next Planning
Commission based on findings made by the Commission.

use in the TMU-2 zone; and
WHEREAS, the Director's determination effectively precludes the proposed 7,000 square-foot
laundromat from operating in the TMU-2 zone under the current land use table, absent a code

 WHEREAS, the Director acknowledges that there is some ambiguity in applying the Laundry

WHEREAS, on April 7th, 2026, the Planning Commission held a duly noticed public hearing to

limitation, the staff report submitted by the Community Development Department and public
testimony; and
WHEREAS, this Resolution and its findings are made based upon the evidence presented to the

NOW, THEREFORE, THE PLANNING COMMISSION DOES HEREBY FIND,
DETERMINE AND DECLARE AS FOLLOWS:
SECTION 1. All of the facts set forth in the recitals above are true and correct and are incorporated
herein by reference.
SECTION 2. Based upon substantial evidence presented to the Planning Commission during the
public hearing conducted with regard to the Applicant's appeal, including the written staff report,
verbal testimony, and all other evidence in the record, the Planning Commission hereby denies
the appeal and upholds the Community Development Director's determination that the proposed
self-service laundromat at 4382–4390 Tweedy Boulevard is classified as a "Dry
Cleaning/Laundry, Plant" use under South Gate Municipal Code Section 11.60.070, based on the
following findings:
  Finding A — The Proposed Use Exceeds the Size Threshold for a Laundry Agency.
  The proposed laundromat is approximately 7,000 square feet, which exceeds the 2,500
  square-foot maximum that distinguishes a Dry Cleaning/Laundry Agency from a Dry
  Cleaning/Laundry Plant under South Gate Municipal Code Section 11.60.070. The size
  threshold established in the Code is an objective, quantifiable standard. Regardless of the
  operational model of the proposed use, the proposed facility's square footage places it
  squarely within the Plant definition under the plain language of the Code.

  29
   Finding B — "Dry Cleaning/Laundry, Plant" Is Not a Permitted Use in the TMU-2
  Zone. The Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan land use table for the TMU-2 zone lists "Dry
  Cleaning/Laundry, Agency" as a permitted use, but does not list "Dry Cleaning/Laundry,
  Plant." Because the proposed facility must be classified as a Plant based on its size, and
  because a Plant is not an identified permitted use in the TMU-2 zone, the proposed use is
  not permitted in the TMU-2 zone under the current land use table.
  Finding C — The Proposed Use Does Not Satisfy the Definition of Personal Services,
  General. The Applicant contends that the proposed laundromat should be classified as
  "Personal Services, General" on the basis that it provides a nonmedical service to
  individuals as a primary use. The Planning Commission finds that this classification is not
  supported by the plain language of the Code. The "Personal Services, General" definition
  and its listed examples such as barber/beauty shops, clothing rental, home electronics and
  small appliance repair, locksmith, pet grooming, shoe repair, tailors, and waxing shops,
  which describe businesses where a trained service provider performs work on behalf of a
  customer. A self-service laundromat, by contrast, provides equipment that customers
  operate themselves to perform their own laundry. While the Commission acknowledges
  that the listed examples are non-exhaustive, the proposed use is more analogous to the Dry
  Cleaning/Laundry category, which the Code specifically created to address laundry-related
  facilities, than to the Personal Services category, which addresses a distinct type of
  customer service business.
  Finding D — Regional Practice and Federal Classification Systems Are Persuasive
  but Not Determinative. The Applicant presented evidence that neighboring jurisdictions
  classify self-service laundromats as personal services or permitted commercial uses, and
  that federal classification systems (NAICS, SIC) assign coin-operated laundromats to a
  category distinct from laundry plants. The Planning Commission finds this evidence
  informative and notes its relevance to the pending code amendment process. However, the
  classification of uses in other cities' zoning codes and federal industry classification
  systems does not govern the interpretation of South Gate's Municipal Code. The
  Commission is bound to apply the Code as currently written.
SECTION 3. The Planning Commission finds that the denial of this appeal does not constitute a
project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) (Public Resources Code Section
21000 et seq.) because it does not approve or authorize any physical development, and no
discretionary approval for development is granted herein. No further CEQA review is required.
SECTION 4. The Planning Commission hereby denies the Applicant's appeal of the Director's
determination and upholds the Director's classification of the proposed self-service laundromat at
4382–4390 Tweedy Boulevard as a "Dry Cleaning/Laundry, Plant" use under South Gate

2. The Misclassification Problem
The City classifies the laundromat under “Dry Cleaning/Laundry” in Section 11.60.070 of the
Zoning Code. That definition has two subcategories:

Agency — “a facility where materials are dropped off and picked up for cleaning service, or
cleaned on site through either conventional laundry or chemical processes where an agency is
less than 2,500 square feet and no material collected at other dry cleaning or laundry agencies
are brought for cleaning.”

Plant — “a facility greater than 2,500 square feet or that processes items collected from other
retail locations, where clothing and similar items are cleaned through either conventional
laundry or chemical processes.”

Both definitions describe a business that performs cleaning as a service for the customer.
Materials are “dropped off and picked up.” The business cleans items through “conventional
laundry or chemical processes.” The 2,500 SF threshold distinguishes a small drop-off location
from a larger processing facility.

A self-service laundromat does none of this. No items are “dropped off.” No items are
“picked up.” The business does not perform any cleaning. Customers bring their own laundry,
operate the machines themselves, and take their items when finished. The 2,500 SF threshold
has no logical application to this model because it was designed to regulate the scale of a
service processing operation, not the customer capacity of a self-service facility.

3. The Correct Classification: Personal Services
After your March 3 meeting, Gabriel Perez emailed Emilia the Personal Services definition from
Chapter 11.60. He stated: “It was mentioned the need for the definitions of personal services.”
This was a clear signal about where to anchor the appeal. The definition reads:

   “Personal Services” (land use) — Section 11.60:
  “Any place of business providing services and accessory retail sales of products related to the
  services provided.”
  General: “Establishments providing nonmedical services to individuals as a primary use. In addition
  to the uses listed below, general personal service uses may also include accessory retail sales of
  products related to the services provided.”
  Examples include: Barber/beauty shop, Clothing rental, Home electronics repair, Locksmith, Pet
  grooming, Shoe repair, Tailor, Waxing shop.
  Fitness/health facility: “Any place of business, or membership club, providing facilities devoted
  especially to health, beauty, and relaxation… including health or physical fitness centers/facilities.”
  Also includes: Instructional uses (art, dance, martial arts, yoga, Pilates, etc.)

3.1 Element-by-Element Analysis
  1. Nonmedical service to individuals as a primary use. Customers come to the facility
  to accomplish a personal task—washing and drying their clothing and household textiles.
  The business provides the service of making commercial-grade equipment available in a
  clean, maintained, professionally attended environment.
  2. Accessory retail sales of products related to the services provided. Laundromats
  sell detergent, fabric softener, dryer sheets, stain removers, and similar products. This
  mirrors how a barber shop sells hair care products or a fitness center sells supplements.
  3. The examples list is non-exhaustive. The code says general personal service uses
  “may also include” the listed examples and uses the word “include”—not “limited to.” A
  self-service laundromat is an unlisted but qualifying example.
  4. The fitness/health facility analogy is directly on point. The code already classifies
  fitness centers as personal services. A gym provides commercial equipment in a
  maintained facility; customers come in, use the equipment themselves, stay for an
  extended period, and leave. A self-service laundromat operates on an identical model.

  commercial streets.

  We respectfully request that the Planning Commission reconsider the classi cation of this
  project and allow the proposed laundromat to move forward as a self-service retail use rather
  than a “planned facility.” Doing so will allow us to deliver a high-quality amenity that bene ts
  both the local community and the surrounding business district.

  Thank you for your time and consideration. We would welcome the opportunity to answer any
  questions and further discuss how this project can positively contribute to the South Gate
  community.

  For the Regular Meeting of: April 7, 2026
Community Development Director:

SUBJECT: STUDY SESSION TO REVIEW PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO THE SOUTH GATE
ZONING CODE FOR 2026

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Receive and File.

DISCUSSION/ANALYSIS:
This study session was continued from the Planning Commission meeting on March 17, 2026.

Planning Division staff identified a work program to update the City of South Gate Municipal Code Title
11, Zoning, to allow greater flexibility in development standards, improve aesthetics in commercial corridors
and city gateways, streamline the development review process, and establish high performance standards
for the built environment. Staff has identified Code Amendments as follows:

Table 11.21-4 Commercial Industrial Zones Allowed Land Uses (Chapter 11.21 Land Use Types)

•  Prohibit Concrete or Cement Manufacturing. Concrete manufacturing uses are only permitted with
  conditional use permit (CUP) approval in the M2 (Light Manufacturing) and M3 (Heavy Manufacturing)
  Zones due to the intensity of the use that involves outdoor storage of cement materials, heavy industrial
  equipment, and regular truck trips. The M2 and M3 zones are concentrated primarily in areas along the
  Union Pacific railroad near the intersection of Firestone Blvd and Atlantic Avenue and East of the 710
  Freeway along Garfield Avenue. Staff recommends amending the Code to prohibit concrete
  manufacturing in the M2 and M3 zones. The code modification would prohibit new cement
  manufacturing businesses and limit expansion of existing cement manufacturing businesses.

•  Modify Vehicle Services, Repair/Storage. Vehicle services repair/storage uses are permitted by-right in
  the M2 and M3 zones and by CUP approval in the IF (Industrial Flex), CDR1 (Corridor 1), CDR2
  (Corridor 2) zones. The proposed amendment prohibits vehicle storage as a primary use only and would
  allow vehicle storage as an accessory use to vehicle repair uses. Outdoor vehicle storage would be
  restricted to rear or side areas of vehicle services buildings where vehicle services are conducted.

•  Vehicle Towing. Vehicle towing services are only permitted by-right in the M2 and M3 zones. Staff
  recommends requiring CUP approval for vehicle towing services in order to ensure towing operations
  maintain public safety, orderly traffic flow on nearby public streets and preserve community aesthetics.

•  Truck Storage/Terminals. Truck storage uses are only allowed by CUP approval in M2 and M3 zones.
  Staff recommends the Planning Commission consider the merits of prohibiting truck storage uses in all

  68
   zones in the City. Truck storage activities may result in noise impacts from truck activity, increased
  traffic congestion, increased air pollution, visual blight, and street pavement impacts.

•  Storage Facilities. Storage facilities are permitted by CUP approval in the LI (Light Industrial) and by-
  right in the M3 zone. Staff recommends prohibiting storage facilities as a primary use, but allowing
  storage facilities as an accessory use in order to preserve land for higher-value and job generating uses.

Table 11.21-3 Allowed Land Uses, Urban Mixed-Use Zones (Chapter 11.21 Land Use Types)

•  Laundromats: Laundromats are currently not listed explicitly as a permitted use. Laundromats were
  previously listed as a conditionally permitted use in Title 11, Zoning, prior to 2015. Staff has relied on
  a determination that laundromats are most similar to “Laundry Agencies” (less than 2,500 sq. ft.) and
  “Laundry Plants” (2,500 sq. ft. or larger), although these terms in other cities are not intended for self-
  service laundry facilities. Staff recommends identifying laundromats on the land use table and allowing
  the use as a conditionally permitted use in the Urban Mixed Use zones with a minimum separation of
  2,500 ft from other laundromats.

Ground-floor retail and pedestrian uses (11.23.070)

•  Storefront Transparency: Staff recommends modifying retail storefront guidelines into standards that
  can be enforced for existing businesses. The guideline currently limits obscuring the view of windows
  by no more than 25%. Additional language would prohibit ground floor windows from being opaque
  or tinted. Product displays would be prohibited from obscuring visibility into the store.

Security Fencing (11.30.070)

•  Security fencing: Barbed wire is identified as a prohibited fencing type in all zoning districts, but is
  prevalent at many industrial businesses throughout the City. Section 11.30.070 provides the ability for
  the Director to consider additional fencing design features in LI, M2, and M3 zoned for security fencing
  on a case-by-case basis. Staff recommends the Planning Commission discuss the existing case-by-case
  security fencing exception. If the Planning Commission were to explore restricting barbed wire
  considerations on a case-by-case basis, staff would recommend that barbed wire fencing be permitted
  on a case-by-case, but restricted to areas not visible from public street view.

Prohibited Signs (11.36.050)

•  Prohibit Cabinet/Box Signs: Staff recommends including cabinet/box signs in the list of prohibited signs
  to improve the visual quality of commercial corridors, reduce bulky signs, encourage higher quality sign
  designs, and prevent excessive illumination.

•  Rooftop Signs. Rooftop signs are currently prohibited and is a commonly adopted prohibition in the
  sign ordinances of other cities. Staff recommends maintaining the prohibition unless approved by the
  Planning Commission as part of a sign program for a major shopping center visible from the 710 or 105
  Freeway and determined to be of a superior architectural design. There are many examples of
  destination commercial areas in California that include rooftop signs that maintain a high aesthetic
  standard and could incentivize economic development activity.

  69
 Signs Allowed by Sign Permit in Commercial and Manufacturing Zone (11.36.050)

•  Establish a permitted sign type: There are no requirements for sign type in the sign ordinance to
  communicate the standard for commercial and industrial signs. Staff recommends establishing a
  standard for channel letters, push-thru, or halo-lit letters as sign alternatives. Painted signs would
  continue to be an allowed sign type when approved by the Director and demonstrated to be designed in
  a superior quality.

•  Establish a sign type standard for freestanding or ground signs. There are no standards for sign type for
  freestanding or ground signs. Staff recommends establishing a standard of channel, routed, halo-lit or
  push-thru letters.

•  Prohibit Pole Signs. Staff recommends prohibiting pole signs to reduce visual clutter along commercial
  corridors, improve community aesthetic and streetscape appearance, and prevent oversized signs that
  dominate the skyline.

Flag Poles in Nonresidential Zoning District (11.40.250)

•  Establish flagpole standards in nonresidential zoning districts: There are no standards for flag poles
  citywide. Staff recommends allowing flag poles at a maximum height of 25 feet by administrative
  approval and establishing a standard for oversized flag poles above 25 feet by city council approval on
  developed sites of a minimum 10 acres.

Appeals (11.50.040)

•  Establish a call-up procedure for decisions under Title 11: There are appeals procedures for decisions
  made by approval authorities pursuant to Title 11, but it is unclear how existing approval authorities can
  appeal decisions of lower decision-making bodies. Staff recommends adding a call-up procedure to
  allow the Planning Commission the ability to call-up administrative decisions and City Council the
  ability to call-up Planning Commission decisions.

CUP Process (11.52.040)

•  Establish CUP expiration: The Zoning code does not establish an expiration for a CUP. Staff
  recommends establishment of a 2-year expiration dates for a CUP and allow three 1-year time extensions
  that can be approved by the Planning Commission.

Lot Line Adjustment (12.02.020)

•  Lot Line Adjustments: A Lot Line Adjustment (LLA) is a process that allows property owners to adjust
  their boundary between adjacent parcels without creating a new lot. The South Gate LLA standards
  require Planning Commission approval, although only tentative parcel and tract maps require Planning
  Commission and Council approval at a public hearing. Surrounding cities of Norwalk, Lynwood,
  Paramount, Downey, and Bellflower allow LLAs by approval of the City Engineer, which reduces the
  processing times for applicants and city staff.

The proposed code amendments will return to the Planning Commission at a future date to be determined
as a formal ordinance for recommendation to the City Council for final consideration and adoption.

11.21.020 General requirements.

All land uses shall conform to the purpose and intent of the applicable zone, and shall
comply with the following:

A. Land Use Operations. No operations conducted on any property shall create
objectionable and/or obnoxious dust, light, matter, mud, noise, odor, refuse, smoke,
steam, vibration, maintenance needs of grounds or buildings, or other nuisance(s). No land
use shall be detrimental to the health and welfare of the South Gate community.

B. Unlisted or Similar Compatible Uses. Any land use that is not specifically listed in the
land use tables for the applicable zone shall not be allowed or permitted within the zone.
However, the director shall have the authority to determine whether the proposed use may
be permitted when all the following findings are made by the director in writing:

1. The characteristics of, and activities associated with, the proposed use are equivalent
to and compatible with one or more of the listed permitted uses, and will not involve a
higher level of activity or density than the permitted uses.

2. The proposed use is substantially similar to a listed permitted use.

3. The proposed use is compatible with the purpose and intent of the applicable zone.

 4. The proposed use has similar traffic, noise, light, odor, and other operational impacts
as a listed permitted use.

5. The operation of the proposed use will not be detrimental to existing uses in the area of
influence.

Decisions of the director may be appealed as described in Chapter 11.50, Administration.

C. Unlisted Use Permit Findings. Consideration of and findings for the determination of
the classification, permissibility, or applicability of an unlisted or similar compatible use,
as defined in subsection (B) of this section, shall be based on the degree of compatibility
between the use in question and adjacent uses. Technical evidence and scientific means,
when available, shall be considered in determining the form and intensity of performance
standards typically associated with any identifiable type of use in question.

D. Unlisted Standards and Permit Requirements. When the director makes the subsection
(B) of this section findings in writing, the proposed use will be treated in the same
regulatory manner as the zone listed use for allowable location(s), permits required, and all
other applicable standards and requirements of this title.

E. Prohibited Uses. For the purposes of public health, safety, and general welfare, land
uses listed in Table 11.21-1 are prohibited in any zone in the city, and are not subject to the
director’s discretion. The city represents a small portion of the entire metropolitan area,
and constitutes a single, economic area of industry and commerce within Los Angeles
County. Full provision is made for all types of uses necessary for industrial development
within the county and thus the following uses, because of their nuisance and hazard
characteristics if permitted within the developed area of South Gate, would defeat the
basic purposes of zoning. The exclusion of these land uses from the city represents a
reasonable regulation, because full provision for the appropriate locations of these uses is
ensured by the total land use pattern of the greater Los Angeles metropolitan area.

11.23.010 Purpose and intent.
The development and design standards and guidelines are organized as a series of sections
that address important design considerations for achieving pedestrian- and human-scaled
development, and reinforcing a sense of place and vibrancy throughout South Gate’s mixed-use
areas. The development and design standards and guidelines outlined in this chapter focus on
overall site planning and development, as well as the overall character and quality of buildings,
retail and pedestrian-oriented development, and the design of building frontages.
Consideration of these standards shall be equally important to the permitted land uses and
development standards identified for each zone.

(Ord. 2323 § 1 Exh. A (part), 4-28-15)

11.23.020 Applicability.
The guidelines of this chapter shall be applicable to the following:

A. All development, redevelopment, expansions, and modifications of buildings and uses
within the urban mixed-use zones.

B.  All mixed-use development projects located in other zones throughout the city.

C. All residential development projects of twenty-one units or more located in any zone
throughout the city.

(Ord. 2323 § 1 Exh. A (part), 4-28-15)

  124
 11.23.030 Notes.
The following notes apply to the development and design standards and guidelines:

A. All standards, dimensions, and requirements identified with mandatory language, including
the words “shall,” “will,” “is to,” and “are to,” are always mandatory. Additional guidelines
provided throughout this chapter, incorporating language such as “should,” indicate that the
standard is not mandatory, but is strongly recommended.

B. Per Section 11.10.080, all standards, dimensions, and requirements of this title are
minimum requirements unless otherwise noted.

C. To provide for flexibility in development and to promote innovative design, administrative
modifications to the standards are permitted, subject to Section 11.30.030, Administrative
modifications.

(Ord. 2323 § 1 Exh. A (part), 4-28-15)

11.23.040 Achieving pedestrian/human-scaled development.
Guidelines for block size, massing, building design, and landscape design are provided within
this title to provide direction on how to create pedestrian-oriented development and a high-
quality public realm. For larger sites, subdivision should first be used to create a connected
network of smaller, pedestrian-scaled blocks and define open space or other special uses. The
following steps are illustrated to help highlight key standards and design strategies.

1. Step 1: Identify Parcel Location and Applicable Zone(s). Review Section 11.20.040, Citywide
zone mapping, to identify the location of your parcel(s), applicable zone(s), and allowable uses.
Review the applicable portions of Chapter 11.22 to identify standards for intensity, building
form, frontage types, and other requirements.

2. Step 2: Define Block Size and Individual Lots. Large sites with vacant blocks or parcels
should be subdivided further to create additional blocks. Subdivision should create a
connected, pedestrian-scaled block and street pattern.

3. Step 3: Identify Alleys. Primary vehicular access to blocks and their individual lots is
preferred along alleys and side streets, except as otherwise allowed within specific zones.

The intent of limiting access to the rear or sides of lots is to maintain the continuity of the
streetscape and pedestrian realm. Additionally, design solutions should minimize the impact of
residential and commercial driveways by using shared driveways, alley access, or other design
approaches to minimize the number of driveways and curb cuts.

  125
 4. Step 4: Define Massing, Circulation, Open Space, and Special Uses. All development
projects, including full-block and half-block projects, should make an attempt to break down
the scale of the development by defining smaller buildings, open space, landscaped setbacks,
pedestrian paths, and paseos.

  A. Special uses such as retail building frontages, pedestrian-oriented uses, and public
  uses should be appropriately considered in the building design. Refer to
  Section 11.23.070 for specific guidelines related to the design of ground-floor retail and
  pedestrian-oriented uses.

  B. All buildings that include residential units are required to comply with the standards
  of Section 11.25.070, Residential operating standards.

5. Step 5: Consider Adjacent Uses and Architectural Compatibility. All development projects,
including full-block and half-block projects, should consider their adjacency to other existing
uses.

  A. The design of mixed-use projects, where sited adjacent to single-family residential
  uses, should incorporate appropriate transitions wherever possible. Acceptable
  transitions include the incorporation of setbacks, open spaces, or upper-story stepbacks.

  126
   B. Architectural unity and harmony should be achieved both within the project, and
  between the project and the surrounding community, so that the project does not
  constitute a disruption to the established fabric of the community. This should be
  considered in the design approach to all buildings, structures, walls, and fences.

  C. All remodeling, modification, expansion, and redevelopment of residential buildings
  should be architecturally compatible with the main building; any required permit for such
  activities shall be conditioned to ensure architectural compatibility.

  D. Sites and structures should be designed to minimize or buffer any undesirable
  characteristics of the site such as street noise and nearby commercial or industrial uses.

6. Step 6: Provide Pedestrian-Scaled Elements. Building massing should be reduced through
changes in building height and roof form, and the introduction of pedestrian-scaled elements.

  A.  Emphasize corners and special places through changes in height and building form.

  B. Incorporate the design of building frontages, per Section 11.23.080, as required in
  specific areas. Over time, the design of building frontages will serve as character-defining
  elements for districts and special places throughout South Gate.

  C. Reduce massing by incorporating pedestrian-scaled elements such as trellises, patios,
  and balconies.

  D.  Limit blank walls and use changes in massing and building planes to add depth and

  scale to building frontages.

7. Step 7: Incorporate Landscape Elements. Incorporate landscape elements and gardens to
define building entries, pathways, and semiprivate open spaces, and to add special character to
building setbacks. Integrate roof-top components such as landscapes gardens, trellises, and
sustainability features. For specific landscape standards, see Section 11.20.070(B)(7).

(Ord. 2323 § 1 Exh. A (part), 4-28-15)

  127
 11.23.050 Open space requirements.
South Gate has a variety of parks and open spaces that provide recreation, relaxation, and
entertainment opportunities. Additional well-designed accessible open spaces sprinkled
throughout the city will create a strong sense of place throughout South Gate, and ensure that
open space is within walking distance of new development.

11.23.060 General building design guidelines.
The following standards underscore basic design principles that are intended to produce high-
quality buildings, memorable places, and a vibrant urban realm. They are not intended to be
indicative of any style, but to encourage innovation and good urban form.

A.  Building Frontage Standards.

  1. Every building should incorporate an allowed frontage type along the lot’s primary
  frontages. Primary frontages include building façades adjacent to a public right-of-way,
  including a public open space such as a plaza, park, or paseo, as well as private open
  space such as a forecourt or courtyard. Allowable frontage types are identified in
  Chapter 11.22 by zone, and detailed in Section 11.23.080.

  2. Residential units should face the street with windows, front entry doors, porches,
  balconies, patios, and stoops. Rooms such as living rooms and dining rooms shall be

  129
   oriented fronting toward the street and/or any adjacent private space. Service rooms and
  areas shall be oriented to the rear of the lot.

  3. Where courtyards, paseos, or greenways exist, residential units should face these
  spaces with windows, front doors, porches, and patios, and according to the standards of
  this section.

B.  Treatment of Building Façades.

  1. Variation and expression of building details, form, line, colors, and materials should
  be used to create visual interest.

  2. Variation in wall plane and roof line is strongly encouraged to reduce the scale and
  bulk of buildings, and to add visual interest.

  3. Individual units should be expressed wherever possible. This may be accomplished in
  a variety of ways, such as through a change in wall plane, change in color, or change in
  roof form.

  4. Street-facing building façades should incorporate pedestrian-scaled elements such as
  balconies, awnings, doors, and windows to enliven the street edge, and increase safety by
  adding eyes on the street.

  5. Blank walls, without windows, doors, or other articulation, are strongly discouraged.
  The maximum length of any blank wall should be limited to twenty feet.

  Development, including residential uses, should address courtyards, paseos, and

  greenways.

  130
  Individual units should be expressed wherever possible. This may be accomplished in a
  variety of ways, such as through a change in wall plane, change in color, or change in

11.23.070 Ground-floor retail and pedestrian-oriented uses.
It is the intent that each zone support a network of interconnected streets and open spaces
that accommodates vehicles while maintaining a balanced physical environment conducive to
pedestrian activity and a walkable street network.

Specific standards for ground-floor retail and pedestrian-oriented uses are identified by zone
within Chapter 11.22. The purpose of regulating these uses is to encourage active land uses in
certain areas such as restaurants, retail stores, civic uses, entertainment, and dining to provide
a vibrant, pedestrian-oriented experience throughout much of the day. These uses are a
defining component of South Gate’s corridors and districts, and serve as key elements of
mixed-use and multistory development.

Pedestrian-oriented uses include active uses that are accessible to the general public, generate
walk-in pedestrian clientele, and contribute to a high level of pedestrian activity in the public
realm. Typical pedestrian-oriented uses include ground-floor retail such as retail shops and
grocery stores, as well as restaurants, outdoor dining areas, bars, theaters, performing arts,
recreation and entertainment, personal and convenience services, building lobbies and building
common areas, civic uses, libraries, museums, galleries, and public plazas.

Along main street areas, such as within the main street zone and the civic center zone,
approximately eighty percent of the ground-floor street fronts should contain active uses. The
guidelines apply only to the ground floor. The director shall consider uses other than retail or
pedestrian-oriented uses in cases of uncertainty or special configurations.

A.  General Requirements for Ground-Floor Retail and Pedestrian-Oriented Uses.

  1. Ground-floor floor-to-ceiling height should be at least ten feet, as measured from the
  adjacent sidewalk, to accommodate retail uses.

  131
   2. Each storefront bay should contain an entrance. The primary entrance to each
  commercial space on the ground floor should be located on the front façade along the
  street.

  3. Architectural features such as canopies, awnings, lighting, and other design features
  should be incorporated into the ground floor to add human scale to the pedestrian
  experience.

  4. Awnings, signs, and other features shall be located at least eight feet above the
  adjacent sidewalk, and may project for the width of the sidewalk to a maximum
  encroachment of within two feet of the curb. Awnings shall only cover individual
  storefronts and openings.

  Each storefront should contain an entrance and glazing.

Building lobbies and common areas should open onto the public right-of-way and can

  add to the pedestrian experience.

  132
 B.  Transparency.

  1. A minimum of sixty percent of the street-facing façades of pedestrian-oriented uses
  should be composed of clear non-reflective glass that allows views of the indoor spaces.

  2. Interior blinds, drapes, posters, signage, and shelving for product displays visible from
  the public right-of-way shallould obscure no more than twenty-five percent of the
  transparent areas of each storefront. Ground-floor windows shall not be opaque or
  tinted. Product displays visible from the inside of the store shall not obscure visibility into
  the storefront from outside the building.

  3. The maximum height of the bottom sill of required display windows should not
  exceed thirty inches above the adjacent sidewalk. The minimum head height for
  storefronts and windows at the ground floor should be eighty inches above the adjacent
  sidewalk.

C. First-Floor Elevation. Pedestrian-oriented uses should have a floor elevation that is level
with the elevation of the adjacent sidewalk.

D. Entrances Facing the Street. Entrances to uses on ground and upper floors should open
onto a public right-of-way. Entrance doors should be set back one to three feet from the
property line.

E. Outdoor Dining. Outdoor dining adjacent to the sidewalk is encouraged. It may be provided
along segments of the building’s front façade that are set back from the property line, or on the
sidewalk. The following requirements shall apply:

  1. All projections into the public right-of-way shall require review and approval by the
  city public works department. See Section 11.40.160 for additional standards.

  2. A continuous, unobstructed path of travel to facilitate pedestrian movement is
  required.

  3.  Outdoor dining shall not be fully enclosed.

F. Vehicular Driveway Access. Vehicular driveway access or entries to parking structures are
discouraged along frontages with active, pedestrian-oriented uses. Access should be taken via
the alleys serving the site or, on corner lots, at the street frontage that does not contain active
ground-floor uses. The director may consider alternate configurations on a project-by-project
basis if such configurations are found to further the goals of the general plan and this title.

  133
   A minimum of sixty percent of the street-facing façades of pedestrian-oriented uses
  should be composed of clear, non-reflective glass, allowing views of indoor spaces.

  Outdoor dining adjacent to the sidewalk is encouraged.

 Entrances should open onto a public right-of-way, with doors set back one to three feet.

11.23.080 Guidelines for building frontage types.
New development should include a range of frontage types to create an interesting pedestrian
environment, add eyes on the street, and define the relationship of building frontages to the
public realm. To add character and to reinforce unique qualities of particular communities,
specific frontage types have been identified by zone, per Chapter 11.22.

  134
 Overall guidelines, applicable to all frontage types, are identified below. Additional guidelines
are identified on the following pages for each specific frontage type.

A.  General Guidelines Applicable to All Frontage Types.

  1. Each building is encouraged to incorporate the frontage types allowed in the
  development standards table for the zone applicable to the site.

  2. Each building should incorporate an allowed frontage wherever the lot’s boundary is
  adjacent to a public right-of-way or an open space such as a plaza, park, or paseo.

  3. Unless specified otherwise, a frontage type should be applied for a lot’s entire primary
  frontage and for at least fifty percent of the side street frontage of a corner lot.

  4.  Ground-floor windows shall not be opaque or tinted.

  5. As allowed by this section, frontage types may be combined, subject to the review and
  approval of the director.

B. Gallery Frontage Type. A gallery is a roof or deck projecting from the façade of a building
and supported by columns. Galleries should typically be located behind the property line and
outside of the right-of-way. A gallery may be combined with other frontage types such as a
front yard, shopfront, or forecourt.

A variety of gallery designs are possible, subject to city approval, per the following, and as
further described in the diagram and photos below.

  1. The height and proportions of the gallery should correspond to the façade and be
  consistent with the architectural style of the building.

  2. The minimum dimensions of a gallery should measure eight feet in width and twelve
  feet in height.

  3. Soffits, columns, and arches should be treated consistent with the architecture of the
  building.

  4. A gallery shall correspond to the openings along the façade(s) to which the gallery is
  being applied.

  5. Where storefront openings are present, spacing between openings along the right-of-
  way should measure between eight and thirty feet in relation to the storefront(s) and the
  height of the ground floor.

  6.  The use of awnings is discouraged with the gallery frontage type.

  136
   7. Street lights are allowed on the face of the gallery columns; provided, that a minimum
  clearance of two feet exists between the light fixture and any adjacent curb face.

  8.  Signage may be applied to the gallery per the requirements of this code.

  9. The gallery frontage type may be subject to the granting of an encroachment permit
  by the city.

11.23.090 Density bonus program.
A. Program Purpose. South Gate has established a density bonus program, permitting
opportunities for increased density, floor area, and/or building height, for projects that provide
public improvements beyond those required by this title. Density bonus incentives are available
for qualified projects subject to review and demonstration of consistency with the incentive
standards of this section, and consistency with the development standards of the applicable
zone.

  145
   1. This density bonus program is separate from the bonus system and standards of
  Chapter 11.31, Density Bonus for Affordable Housing.

  2. Chapter 11.22, Urban Mixed-Use Zones, identifies a “maximum with bonus” in the
  Development Standards tables for each zone.

  i. The “maximum with bonus” is applicable only to incentives specified in this
  section.

  ii. The “maximum with bonus” may not be achievable on all sites, as site conditions
  or superseding development regulations may reduce development potential.

  iii. Density bonuses for affordable housing shall be permitted to exceed the
  “Maximum with Bonus” in accordance with Government Code Section 65915 et seq.,
  and as amended.

B.  Program Regulation.

  1. Computation of Density Bonuses. The percentages of all the bonus options identified
  in Table 11.23-3 for the project shall be added together. The total shall then applied to the
  number of units, to determine the additional units allowed.

  2. Interpretation. The planning director shall have discretion to determine the total
  density bonus accrued, based on consistency with the intent of the density bonus
  program and the magnitude of benefit or amenity with respect to the development size.
  The planning commission shall approve the bonus determination.

  3. Maximum Bonus. The maximum bonus allowed for the provision of improvements or
  amenities, as identified in subsection (C) of this section, shall be limited to the available
  “maximum with bonus” as regulated in the development standards of that zone.

  4. Compliance with Standards. All requirements of the density bonus program must be
  met in full to receive the bonus. The applicant shall document all of the density bonus
  requirements that are met. Documentation is required prior to the issuance of building
  permits for bonus units.

  5. Covenants. The applicant must sign a covenant that ensures that the improvements
  or amenities provided to achieve any density bonus will continue to be provided for the
  life of the project.

C. Incentives. Refer to Table 11.23-3 for a summary of improvements or amenities that may
be provided as density bonus incentives, as well as related requirements and available density
increases. In order to be eligible for the density bonus program, projects shall either (1)
incorporate a child day care facility, or (2) contribute two or more public improvements or

The purpose of this chapter is to specify the requirements and development standards within
the residential neighborhood zones as established by the zoning map. Residential
neighborhood zones are established to provide areas suitable for residential living and civic
activities, to protect the character and form of existing residential neighborhoods of South
Gate, and to minimize the impacts and noise of adjacent nonresidential uses on residential
neighborhoods.

(Ord. 2323 § 1 Exh. A (part), 4-28-15)

11.25.020 Applicability.
The building, design, and development standards of this chapter shall be applicable to all
buildings and uses within the residential neighborhood zones and multifamily developments in
mixed-use zones.

  150
 (Ord. 2323 § 1 Exh. A (part), 4-28-15)

11.25.030 Residential neighborhood character.
Residential neighborhood zones are characterized differently than other zones for the purpose
of protecting and extending the unique residential character of the existing South Gate
neighborhoods. Residential neighborhood zones include neighborhood low (NL), neighborhood
medium (NM), civic (CV), and open space (OS) zones. The specific design and development
standards for each zone are detailed within this chapter. Residential neighborhood zone
development standards and site planning standards are intended to regulate, create, maintain,
and preserve residentially focused areas with civic, recreation, and open space amenities.

(Ord. 2323 § 1 Exh. A (part), 4-28-15)

11.25.040 Allowable uses.
A. Land Uses. Residential uses are intended to be the primary permitted use in all residential
neighborhood zones. Allowable uses in residential neighborhood zones, as identified by Table
11.21-5, Residential Neighborhood Zone Allowed Land Uses, shall be for the express purpose of
establishing high-quality residential living environments and minimizing the impacts and
nuisance of non-residential uses.

B. Home Occupations. Home occupations shall be permitted in conjunction with any
residential land use in the NL, NM, and MH zones, subject to the provisions of this code.

(Ord. 2323 § 1 Exh. A (part), 4-28-15)
